one_line: Fixed cameras plus a staff-phone walk that finds empty facings, planogram breaks and wrong shelf tags in independent grocers and specialty retailers, then turns POS velocity into a ranked restock/tag-fix list.

problem.summary: Small independents run shelf checks by eye, once a day at best, by whoever is free. Industry data says roughly 6.5% of grocery items are out of stock at a given moment nationally (2023), while independents' own survey respondents reported an average out-of-stock rate of 17.5% (FY2022), and 'empty shelves' is the top reason grocery shoppers leave without buying. Price-tag accuracy is not optional in New Jersey: merchants must clearly mark prices, the state has a mandatory unit-pricing law, and the Attorney General has extracted two seven-figure settlements from chains over tag/register and unit-price mismatches. Independents carry the cost with thin labor: 186 supermarkets in Middlesex County average ~32 employees (5,902 employees / 186 establishments) and ~$33k average annual pay, and single-store grocers run ~1.5% EBITDA.

evidence.fact: Grocery out-of-stock rate fell from 10.7% in 2022 to 6.5% in 2023, below the ~8% historical norm, per FMI's Food Retailing Industry Speaks.

Independent grocers surveyed by FMS/NGA reported an average out-of-stock rate of 17.5% in FY2022, down from 24.3% in 2021, and 49% said they lost sales to procurement problems — a much higher out-of-stock level than the national all-retailer figure above.

IHL Group put inventory distortion at $1.77T globally (2023 study), with $349B in lost sales for U.S./Canadian retailers in 2022 and 17.7% more out-of-stocks in North America than the prior year; for food/grocery, 'empty shelves' was the number one reason shoppers gave for leaving without intended purchases.
New Jersey law requires merchants to clearly mark the price of items either on the item or on the display where it is offered for sale.

New Jersey is one of nine states with a mandatory unit-pricing law; the AG's Office of Weights and Measures found more than 2,000 unit-of-measure errors at Walmart's 64 NJ stores in Q1 2023, producing a $1.64M settlement with a $1.61M civil penalty.

OWM inspections of 58 Dollar General stores (Nov 2022, Feb 2023) found more than 2,000 items scanning higher than the posted price, in some cases by $5.95; the chain paid $1.2M (including a $1.18M civil penalty) and must internally audit every NJ store yearly, with >2% overcharges in a sample counting as a failed audit.

Middlesex County had 186 NAICS 445110 (supermarket) establishments in 2024 with 5,902 average employees, $195.8M total annual wages, average annual pay $33,172 and average weekly wage $638; NAICS 4451 overall had 333 establishments and 7,002 employees, and NAICS 44513 (convenience) had 147 establishments.

Independent grocers' FY2024 net profit edged up to 1.9%, but EBITDA was 1.52% for single-store operators versus 3.28% for multi-store/higher-volume operators; labor and benefits hit a record 16.3% of net sales (survey: 93 respondents / 626 stores, plus benchmarks from 507 grocers).
Independent grocers reported 57% average store-level staff turnover, and 35% said they were using automation to fill labor gaps (survey: 521 grocers representing nearly 2,000 stores).

In a vendor case study, a national grocery retailer's existing manual gap-scan process found only 35.6%, 52.3% and 57.1% of shelf gaps across three stores, versus 93.3%, 95.2% and 93.9% for the camera-based scan (vendor-reported).

buyers.size_where_it_matters: ~5,000–40,000 sq ft, 10–40 aisles, 15+ staff; 186 such establishments in Middlesex County (2024)

buyers.why: Narrow aisles and 1–3 staff on shift, so no one walks the aisles; small planograms make a 20–30 camera-free capture cheap. (inference)

buyers.business_type: Specialty food retail: meat markets, produce markets, bakeries, ethnic grocers
buyers.why: Perishable, high-turn categories where a hole is a lost sale today, and where staff already handle price changes by hand. (inference)
Large facings-per-SKU and heavy promo/tag churn; price accuracy matters because unit pricing and posted-price rules apply to regulated commodities. (inference)
Planogram-driven front store with vendor compliance expectations; staff time goes to resets rather than daily gap walks. (inference)

buyers.why: Same gap problem without grocery's perishable urgency; price-tag accuracy still matters for posted-price rules, and planograms are simpler to digitize. (inference)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Scans 15–30K products per hour, up to 3x/day (a large supermarket takes 1.5–2 hours per scan), reporting which products are not on shelf and which facings are missing; generates a 'realogram' when the store has no accurate planogram; API for downstream systems.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown — Robot-as-a-Service: zero upfront cost, monthly fee depending on store size, SKU count and whether CV and/or RFID is used; company says most of its stores are >5,000 sq ft (minimum >1,000 sq ft)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Shelf-mounted cameras sold as an AI-as-a-Service for grocery, convenience, pharmacy and health-and-beauty; vendor says a store installs in a single day, cameras take still images and pixels containing individuals are stripped before analysis or storage, and the vendor maintains the hardware.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown — set-up fee plus a monthly service fee; total depends on number/size of stores, number of services and contract length. Cameras are not sold separately (AI-as-a-Service).

existing_solutions.product: Shelf availability scanning (mobile/drone capture + cloud CV)
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Captures shelf images with handheld or drone devices and reports gaps and shelf conditions; vendor case study claims 94% gap-detection accuracy and 99% overall accuracy versus 35.6–57.1% for the retailer's existing manual scan, and ~2 s vs >6 s per shelf segment.

Autonomous aisle-scanning robot with built-in lighting so it can scan with store lights off, an 8-hour scanning shift, high-resolution cameras for price tags, depth sensors for shelf-out detection, an overhead camera that captures overhead stock up to 7 m high, and optional RFID.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown — no published price; a distributor listing describes acquisition via written quote or robot-as-a-service (robot-distribution.com/en/brands/zippedi)

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Per-store, per-SKU order recommendations for fresh and now center-store using POS, inventory, waste and promo history — the 'reorder tied to POS' half of this avenue without the shelf-vision half.
existing_solutions.pricing: Unknown (demo/quote; positioned at regional and national grocery chains)

existing_solutions.product: YOLO11/YOLO models, SKU-110K dense-shelf dataset pipeline
existing_solutions.what_it_does: Open detector family used to find product facings and shelf edges; SKU-110K (11,743 densely packed shelf images) is the standard pretraining set for product detection.
existing_solutions.pricing: Free under AGPL-3.0; paid Enterprise license required for closed-source/commercial embedding, price not published

existing_solutions.what_it_does: Local NVR whose object-detector plugin runs YOLO-family models via OpenVINO, TensorRT, ONNX or Edge TPU, including custom label maps — usable as the detection layer behind fixed shelf cameras. Camera ingest (RTSP/ONVIF) and per-camera zone definitions live in separate docs pages.

gap_for_local_installer: Every credible shelf-intelligence vendor is built for chains: robots that need wide aisles and 5,000+ sq ft, cloud RaaS contracts, and enterprise sales cycles. Independents have no accurate planograms (Simbe's own FAQ says most retailers don't), legacy POS with no clean API, and 1.5% single-store EBITDA, so a per-store enterprise subscription rarely pencils. A local installer can sell the inverse: on-prem capture (4–8 fixed PoE cameras on the fastest aisles plus a 5-minute staff phone walk for the rest), build the realogram from the store's own shelf images in week one, wire alerts into the tasks the staff already do, and price it as a flat monthly service call rather than a platform contract. The defensibility is the per-store calibration set, the shelf-tag/label dictionary, and the fact that nobody else will drive to Milltown for a 12,000 sq ft account.

technical_approach.established_pattern: Two published patterns dominate: (a) detect every product facing with a dense object detector, then infer gaps from missing positions, and (b) directly detect empty shelf space as its own class — the paper below reports that pattern (a) cannot see 'frontal' gaps that are boxed in from behind, and that pattern (b) with a second frontal class scores higher. Both are followed by shelf-row/sequence alignment against a planogram or a learned 'realogram', then tag reading to catch price mismatches. Published work runs this on a walking robot or a phone/cart capture rather than continuous fixed cameras, because one camera covers only a few feet of shelf (inference from camera geometry, not from a cited test). For a small store the practical hybrid is: fixed cameras on the 10–20% of facings that carry most velocity (always-on, cheap), plus a once- or twice-daily phone or cart-mounted capture for full-store coverage, with a small VLM used only to adjudicate ambiguous frames and read tags.

technical_approach.fine_tuning_needed: Yes for the detector, no for the VLM. Shelf/product detection needs a store-specific fine-tune: start from SKU-110K-style pretraining, then 300–800 hand-labeled shelf images per store (a few categories at a time). Do not promise a headline AP jump: the peer-reviewed study below gained ~4 AP points on the normal class over the best prior deep-learning baseline, so the win for a client is workflow and coverage, not a new accuracy record. The VLM is usable as shipped for tag reading and ambiguous-frame triage (Liquid documents LoRA recipes for the 1.6B, with the caveat that the vendor recommends fine-tuning for best results); only a light LoRA is worth it if a store has unusual label formats. Planogram data is the real work: expect to build the realogram manually from captured images (hours per store) because independents rarely have usable planograms.

measured_outcomes.finding: Direct detection of empty shelf space with a two-stage (augment-then-fine-tune) training process plus an aspect-ratio post-filter reached 86.3% AP on fully empty out-of-stocks and 83.7% AP on 'frontal' out-of-stocks (85.0 mAP across both classes). That is about 4 AP above the best prior deep-learning direct-detection baseline (Jha et al.: YOLOv5 82.4%, YOLOv7 79.7%, EfficientDet 77.1% on the normal class) and far above earlier classical detectors (Canny 63.8%, colour histogram 61.4%, SVM 56.9%).
measured_outcomes.sample: 511 full-height shelf images from four major retailers in Croatia; 1,210 labeled OOS instances (730 normal, 480 frontal); 5-fold test

measured_outcomes.finding: A shelf-scanning robot (ROSCH) was 8x faster than a human operator at routine out-of-stock detection while running during store hours.
measured_outcomes.sample: ~2,000 annotated images (900 captured in 3 Italian supermarkets); tested in 1 supermarket in Salerno

measured_outcomes.finding: Camera-based gap scanning found 93.3%, 95.2% and 93.9% of gaps in three stores, versus 35.6%, 52.3% and 57.1% for the retailer's existing manual process; Pensa reported 94% gap-detection and 99% overall accuracy, and ~2 s versus >6 s per shelf segment.

measured_outcomes.sample: Inserra Supermarkets' 23 ShopRite stores and ShopRite Supermarkets Inc.'s 37 ShopRite locations in NY and NJ, within the Wakefern co-op

legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey's Wiretap Act is one-party consent: intercepting an oral communication without a party's consent is a crime (N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-3/-4). Practical rule for a shelf system: buy cameras with microphones disabled or absent, and never record audio.

legal_privacy.issue: Whether video-only recording falls under the Wiretap Act
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: New Jersey courts have held the video portion of a recording is outside the Wiretap Act (State v. Diaz, 1998, discussing N.J.S.A. 2A:156A-2); the Act covers aural interception.

NJ requires prices to be clearly marked on the item or the display; N.J.A.C. 13:47C-3.5 sets a penalty of not less than $100 per violation, and each package in violation is a separate violation under N.J.S.A. 51:1-100. New Jersey also mandates unit pricing (one of nine states).

NJ OWM inspections produced a $1.2M Dollar General settlement (announced November 2023) with a mandated annual internal audit where >2% overcharges = failed audit, and a $1.64M Walmart unit-pricing settlement (June 2024) with the same 2% audit-failure threshold. A tag-verification product has a documented regulatory driver, not just a shrink argument.

The New Jersey Data Privacy Law (effective Jan 15, 2025) applies only to controllers processing personal data of 100,000+ NJ consumers (or 25,000+ plus data sales), so a 5–200 staff retailer is generally out of scope — but the system should still avoid collecting customer-identifiable data.

legal_privacy.issue: Facial recognition / biometric surveillance in stores
legal_privacy.rule_or_precedent: STATUS: introduced bill, not confirmed law. NJ A3929 (2026 session) would make it an unlawful practice to run facial or other remote biometric recognition on consumers at a business's premises unless it gives clear and conspicuous notice and uses the system for a lawful purpose, with a 30-day cure after a first violation and a bar on selling or sharing the resulting data. I read the bill text only and could not confirm enactment or committee action, so this must not be treated as current law. Recommendation: build no face recognition at all.

FTC's May 2023 policy statement says misuse of biometric information — including false claims about accuracy and bias/discrimination risk — can be an unfair or deceptive practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

NLRB General Counsel Memo GC 23-02 (Oct 31, 2022) targets electronic monitoring and algorithmic management that interferes with employees' Section 7 rights — relevant because shelf cameras also observe staff, and because gap alerts can become performance metrics.

I could not confirm any New Jersey statute that requires notice to employees for video-only recording in non-private work areas; recommended practice is posted signage and a written policy even where not mandated.

I could not confirm a New Jersey-specific retention limit for retail video; the defensible posture is short retention (e.g., 7–30 days for raw frames), keeping only derived shelf-state metadata, and no cloud upload by default. Note that at least one vendor (Focal) says it strips pixels containing individuals before analysis or storage — a design pattern worth copying.

The product flags shelves, not people, which keeps it clear of biometric and defamation exposure; the residual risk is blaming a named employee for an unfilled gap based on a false positive, so alerts should be shelf- and task-centric with a human confirmation step. (inference)

public: Google/Yelp reviews that mention specific empty shelves, 'couldn't find', or a price that rang up higher than the tag (a recurring phrase pattern is the strongest low-cost signal). (inference)
Weekly circular size and page count — more advertised items means more tag changes per week and more chances for a mismatch. (inference)
Store footprint and aisle count published on the store's own site or in a shopping-center lease flyer; 8+ aisles with 15+ staff is where a walk stops happening. (inference)
Number of locations (1–10 is the sweet spot; above that they are already talking to Simbe/Focal). (inference)

Co-op/wholesaler affiliation visible on signage or the site (Wakefern/ShopRite, Key Food, IGA, Associated) — Wakefern members may already get shelf tools through the co-op (Simbe's Tally is deployed at two Wakefern members), so prioritize non-Wakefern banners.
Job postings for 'price integrity', 'planogram', 'reset crew' or overnight stocker roles — evidence that tag/shelf labor is a named, unfilled job. (inference)
NJ Division of Consumer Affairs / OAG press releases and OWM enforcement actions naming a banner (public, but only large chains appear).
Store photos on Google Maps that show empty facings, handwritten price signs or cases sitting in the aisle. (inference)
walk_in: Holes with no shelf tag versus holes with a tag — the first is a stocking gap, the second is a planogram/price gap; count both per aisle for 10 minutes.
Handwritten, taped or expired promo signs; tag facings that don't match the product in front of them.
Overstock on top stock or cut cases parked in the aisle (a sign the store restocks from the back by memory, not by list). (inference)
Number of staff on the floor at 2–4 pm and whether anyone carries a handheld scanner or a printed pick list.
Existing camera domes: count them, check whether they are IP/ONVIF (label on the housing) and whether any point at shelves rather than the door.
Register/POS model and receipt format — can you get an item-level sales export, or is the only data a Z-report? (inference)
Paper shelf tags versus electronic shelf labels; ESLs mean the price half of the pitch is already solved and only availability remains. (inference)
Backroom: is there a labeled location for each overstock item, or is it floor-stacked? (inference)

pilot.scope: One store, 2–4 weeks. Week 1: baseline — two manual gap/price audits per day for five days on a fixed 10–15 aisle route, plus a POS item-level export. Week 2: install 4 fixed PoE cameras on the highest-velocity aisles, build the realogram from captured images, label 300–500 shelf images, fine-tune the detector. Weeks 3–4: daily operation — one 5-minute phone walk per shift plus continuous fixed-camera monitoring on priority aisles, alerts pushed to the store's existing task channel, weekly review of precision and missed holes against a spot audit.
pilot.hardware: 4x 4K PoE cameras (list $80–$200 / current $48–$120 each), PoE switch, one Jetson Orin Nano Super ($249, supports up to four cameras so this is the ceiling for a single Jetson) or an Intel mini-PC as the local inference box, existing staff phone for the walk, cart/phone mount, cabling. Everything on-prem; no cloud dependency, no audio capture.
pilot.success_metric: Primary: at least 25% fewer empty facings on the audited route at the 2 pm audit versus baseline. Secondary: ≥90% of gap alerts confirmed real by staff (precision), price-tag mismatch count reduced by half, and ≤10 minutes/day of added staff time. (thresholds are targets, not findings)
pilot.cost_range: $4,500–$9,500 for the pilot: cameras plus Jetson $440–$730 at the prices cited above, plus an unsourced allowance for switch, cabling, mounts and labor (assume $700–$1,600 all-in hardware), 35–55 hours of build/install/labeling at $100–$125/hr ($3,500–$6,900), plus travel. Ongoing service after the pilot: $300–$700/month per store. Assumes one store, 10–15 aisles, existing Wi-Fi or a $150–$300 cabling run, client supplies POS export, and no custom hardware enclosure.
pilot.assumptions: Assumes the store will give a POS export (CSV or API) and 30 minutes of staff time on day one; assumes an 8–15k sq ft sales floor with 2.1–2.4 m shelving; excludes electronic shelf labels, excludes any customer analytics, and assumes the detector fine-tune reaches roughly 80–86% AP on the store's own images — the low end of what the Croatian study reports, because US packaging and lighting differ (inference). If labeling needs exceed 800 images, add 15–25 hours.

fit_score.rationale: The problem is real and measurable (national out-of-stock 6.5% in 2023 while independents self-report 17.5%, empty shelves the top reason grocery shoppers leave, mandated price marking plus two seven-figure NJ settlements), and Middlesex County alone has 186 supermarkets and 147 convenience establishments. But independents run ~1.9% net profit, 1.52% single-store EBITDA and 16.3% labor cost, so willingness to pay is the constraint, not the technology: ~86% AP on empty-shelf detection is published and reachable with a YOLO fine-tune, but the gain over the best prior deep-learning baseline is only ~4 AP, and fixed cameras see just a few feet of shelf, so the phone walk is load-bearing. Video-only sensing with no audio and no biometrics keeps legal risk modest (NJ privacy law thresholds not met), though employee-monitoring and notice questions remain unconfirmed. Defensibility is the weak leg — enterprise vendors and open-source stacks both exist, and electronic shelf labels solve the price-tag half more directly — so the moat has to be local installation, per-store calibration data and service, not the model.

risks: Independents may not pay a recurring fee for a problem they have tolerated for years; the value story has to be price-accuracy penalty avoidance and night-crew hours, not 'AI'.
Most independents have no accurate planogram (Simbe says as much), so the installer absorbs the cost of building a realogram — unbilled hours in the first store of every account.
False positives erode trust fast; if staff chase 10 bad alerts they stop using the list within a week.

Fixed cameras are a poor fit for full-store coverage (a few feet of shelf per camera, and a single Jetson Orin Nano Super accepts up to four cameras), so the phone walk is load-bearing and depends on staff compliance.
The accuracy pitch is thinner than it looks: the peer-reviewed benchmark beats prior deep-learning baselines by only ~4 AP, so selling on model performance rather than workflow is a losing argument.
Electronic shelf labels already solve tag accuracy for chains and are dropping in price; the pitch must lead with availability and planogram execution, not just price checks.
Wakefern/ShopRite members may get shelf tools through the co-op (Simbe's Tally is already deployed at Inserra and SRS), narrowing the addressable base.
POS integration is the hidden cost: legacy registers may only export end-of-day totals, which weakens the reorder ranking.
Cameras that also capture employees invite NLRA Section 7 scrutiny and morale problems if alerts become de facto performance metrics.
VLM price reading can hallucinate a digit; any price change must be human-confirmed before it reaches a shelf tag or the POS.
caveats: Vendor outcome claims (Pensa, Simbe, Zippedi, Focal) are rated Low and were not independently audited; vendor accuracy and speed figures are self-reported. All published detection-accuracy figures come from small datasets outside the US (Croatia, Italy), so local accuracy on US packaging and shelf formats is an extrapolation. Middlesex County establishment counts come from BLS QCEW 2024 annual averages and include chains, not just independents; the count of independents with 5–200 staff is an estimate. Hardware prices are street/list prices seen on the cited pages at the time of research and will move, and the switch/cabling/mount allowance is unsourced. NJ A3929 is a bill, not law. No store visits, interviews or customer discovery were performed for this brief.
data_gaps: No public pricing for Simbe, Focal, Pensa, Zippedi or Afresh — all quote-only, so per-store ROI cannot be benchmarked against their actual contracts.
No published New Jersey or Middlesex County out-of-stock rate; the FMI figure is national and the 17.5% figure is a national independent-grocer survey, not local.
Could not retrieve Census County Business Patterns for Middlesex County (API requires a key); used BLS QCEW instead, which does not break out establishment size classes.
No peer-reviewed US deployment of fixed-camera shelf monitoring in an independent grocery; the closest evidence is a 3-store vendor case study.
Could not confirm any NJ statute requiring employee notice for video-only CCTV, nor a NJ-specific video retention limit.
Status of NJ bill A3929 (biometric surveillance notice) beyond introduced text was not verified; treat as pending, not law.
NJ OWM store-level inspection results are not public in a searchable form (only the sticker-verification portal for individual devices), so price-accuracy risk cannot be scored per prospect.
No data found on how many Middlesex County independents run POS systems with usable APIs versus closed legacy registers.
No vendor price opened for PoE switches, cabling, mounts or a dedicated capture phone, so those pilot line items are allowances rather than quotes.
